claim: Koijen, Richmond & Yogo's demand-system estimate finds that the shift in the wealth distribution across institutional investors from 2007.Q4 to 2016.Q4 (the active-to-passive transition) produced an economically significant counterfactual repricing of the AGGREGATE market of 14%, over a 9-year window.
stance_target: Passive/index flows mechanically support equity valuation levels independent of fundamentals
scope_conditions: aggregate cross-section of the largest 90% of US firms by market equity, pooled
quoted_support:
We ﬁnd an economically signiﬁcant
estimate of 14%.

claim: The estimated demand system shows price elasticity of demand is low on average across institutional investor types and ranges from 0 to 1; even hedge funds -- the most price-elastic institutional investor type -- have a wealth-weighted price elasticity of only about 0.5.
stance_target: Equity markets are highly inelastic, so flows move prices far more than efficient-market models predict
scope_conditions: estimated by investor type/group, not by individual stock
quoted_support:

claim: The decline in the aggregate institutional active share from 38.9% (2007.Q4) to 32.8% (2016.Q4) is decomposed into a -1.3 percentage-point contribution from investment strategies becoming more passive and a larger -4.8 percentage-point contribution from capital flowing from active to passive investors (i.e., changes in the wealth distribution, not changed behavior) -- meaning the mechanical/flow-driven component is roughly 3.7x the size of the behavioral component.
stance_target: Passive/index flows mechanically support equity valuation levels independent of fundamentals
scope_conditions: aggregate market, institutional investors present in both 2007.Q4 and 2016.Q4
quoted_support:
We ﬁnd that the change in the aggregate active share is the sum of −1.3% for the
ﬁrst term and −4.8% for the second term.
